utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. First, I would like to say good morning to everybody and to be sure that everybody can hear me. Do the interpreters hear me? Yes. Good morning. Very well. I won't ask you, Mr. Registrar, to have the accused brought in because we just learned that the accused is ill; he saw a physician. I was also concerned about whether he would give his counsel his consent for the hearings to proceed without him. Mr. Greaves, I believe that the consent was given; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I understand both from my learned friend, Mr. Londrovic, who has spoken to him today, and from Mr. Rohde of the Defence counsel liaison unit, who has also been in communication with him, that he has indicated, for the time being, that he is prepared for the trial to continue without him. Whether that remains the case throughout or he changes his mind in regard to tomorrow, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that according to what Mr. Rohde said to me, this would hold for the whole day because the physician said that he should rest all day long. I don't really think that we're not going to be able to continue without him -- that we are going to -- we have to continue without him all through the day, but we can do that once you've been given the consent of the accused; isn't that correct, Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I spoke with Goran by telephone this morning. As a matter of fact, he called me and told me that he had some problems last night, it is probably his stomach or ulcer, and tomorrow he is to have his blood taken for analysis. But in view of the situation the victims are in and that they have to stay in The Hague, yes, he said that he would be quite prepared to have the trial go on today without him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I would, first of all, like to say good morning to Witness K and ask how Witness K feels. Mr. Goran Jelisic is being taken care of. People are paying attention to him. He has that right, that right recognised to him, not only to be ill but not to attend part of his only trial. The Judges, and my colleagues agree with me, first of all, tell me that I would like to turn to the witness and ask the witness how she feels today. How do you feel today, Madam? Do you feel better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... force myself. I have to do it. I feel a lot of pain.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the second witness's microphone put on too, please, and brought closer to her?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that this is a very difficult and painful moment for you. What I ask is that if you don't feel well, just stop, ask us to stop, and we will suspend the hearing. The accused isn't here for the reasons that have been explained. I think that you should be able to manage to feel more serene. If you don't, you can stop and you can count on all of us who are here, that's including Defence counsel. Mr. Nice, if you would continue, please, with the sensitivity which you know how to demonstrate in this type of case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness K, I think there's been some discussion or consideration given to whether you would find it easier to give your evidence in English or in Bosnian. It may be that you've decided that you'll be happier at least to try speaking in Bosnian and listening over the headphones; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then take your time. I'll speak to you, of course, in English because I'm afraid I don't speak your language, and then listen to the question as it comes over the headphones in Bosnian, the channel is on the Bosnian language, and then if you reply in Bosnian, we'll all listen to it in our own languages and we'll make progress that way. You'd reached the position yesterday of telling us how Ranko Cesic had made you sit down in front of him in that little room. Incidentally, we can deal with this all very quickly, so don't worry about details very much. Just tell us what he did while you were in that room. I think it had something to do with a gun.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, I forgot to mention a small incident. He brought in a man before he started beating us, the people from the hospital. He brought in a man from the hangar. He was so beaten up that he was all bloody. Blood was gushing from his face and it was gushing to such an extent that you could not recognise his face. Since I was so frightened, I forgot to mention that yesterday, and I would like to mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's helpful. Now we can go back to the second incident. When you'd been asked by him to sit down, just tell us, in a sentence, what he did with the gun.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was shooting around my body. It was so close that I felt the heat of the bullets and the smell of gun powder. He was so arrogant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. So --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was so irritating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll move to the next little bit. Then I think you left the room with this man, and perhaps we can put that plan on the ELMO again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I gather, Your Honour, for various reasons, that when the plan is being used, we'll see it or we can follow it, but it won't, I think, be available to the public for the usual reasons. I'm not sure how the technical side of things works, but apparently that's what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you went out this time, Witness K, did you go on foot or did you get into a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went on foot to the vehicle together with him, and he brought me into the vehicle. I sat on the seat next to him. Behind my head were two big dogs, and he told them to snarl behind my neck. He started the car, he came to the gate, and he ordered the guards to open the gate. The guards opened the gate, and the vehicle went towards the hangar. I can show you the direction that he drove. He entered at this gate [indicating]. We went slowly around. He drove slowly all around here [indicating]. So the dogs were snarling. He did not say much. He grinned ironically. But I saw a lot of civilians around, and their hands were put above their heads on the walls. I cannot describe my fear to you, and I cannot give you the exact number of people, but I saw that there were quite a few people, and most of them were men, it seems to me, men in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you came out of the hangar, did he drive out of the camp some distance to a secluded area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I got out of the hangar. Then we came to the gate, and the guards there knew him. Since they knew him, they opened up quickly, and we went out in this direction [indicating], towards the bridge that had been blown up. It was already getting dark. I panicked terribly, because I knew that this was the end of the road. I knew that the bridge was no longer there. I didn't know what would happen afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he have a weapon with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had an automatic rifle, he had a knife on the side, and I even think he had a pistol at his belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When he stopped the car, was it in a secluded area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was near the bridge where it was dark and that was the end of the street that led to the River Gunja. On the other side was Gunja, that's the Croat part, and that was the end of the road and that's where we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you can tell us a bit, if you like, just literally in one sentence, because I don't want any detail. Tell us in one sentence what he did and then we'll move on to the next.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me that he decided, way back in the office as he was shooting at me and playing with my nerves, he said what he would do to me. He got a knife out. First he put the knife here and he cut off a button with the knife. He raised my uniform a bit and then he put the knife underneath my neck and he said that I should not move, otherwise, he would slit my throat in a single move. The dogs were snarling behind my back, and I could feel their froth. I just firmly held -- I just firmly, firmly held onto the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He pulled me in a semi-lying position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think, in a sentence, and I'm going to put this to you and you don't have to give any detail: I think he raped you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When he'd done that, what did he say he was going to do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he had finished the first part and that we would move on to the second part. He was buttoning himself up, closing the door, and he said to me that we should move to the river bank and that he would slit my throat there and throw me into the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did another vehicle arrive at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, when he was talking to me, I heard and saw the light -- heard a car. I think I saw the lights of a car. I saw the light. I'm not sure I heard the vehicle. There was light on us, and a man came out of the car and called out to him loud, telling him to get out, that he wanted to talk to him. He called out his name and surname, and that is when I first heard his name and surname. He called out to him two or three times, and he was quarrelling with him. However, Ranko did not want to react to what he was saying. He wanted to do his own thing, what he wanted to do, but the man insisted. It's not that they were fighting physically, but they argued a lot and they were very loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Eventually, did the men or man who just arrived get you to go into their car and take you to the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this man who was arguing with him a lot, and he was keeping him, whereas the other man went to the other side. He opened the door and said in a very calm voice to me, "Please Madam, could you get out and move into our vehicle? And please don't be afraid. We don't want to hurt you." But as I was passing by, I heard that the man who talked to Ranko was saying to him that he did not have permission to take victims out without a written permit. As I was passing by, I heard that bit of conversation. Then I moved to the other car, and they closed door and I sat on the back seat. So I don't know what they were talking about afterwards, but they remained in conversation or, actually, I saw them speaking. Then we left and the man started driving towards the SUP in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, Witness K, you can deal with these matters very shortly if you like, and it will probably help if you deal with it very shortly. At the police station were you questioned? If so, just tell us the topics that you were questioned about, but do it in a sentence, if you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, I waited and I saw lots of policemen, soldiers. They were milling about all over. But I had to wait until the chief of police would be available. This man who brought me in, his name was Dragan. He talked to me. He tried to calm me down. He offered me coffee, and he said that this was only an informative talk, interview, and that I should not be afraid. After 15 minutes or so, he said to me that we could leave, and he took me to the third floor where the chief of police was. This was like a conference room. There were four men there and there was a guard. Across the door a chair was offered to me, and across from that chair sat the chief of police, and at the bottom of the table there were two other men. So I did not really pay attention to them, and I didn't realise whether I knew them or not. I was probably afraid as well. I did not recognise anyone. The chief of police, who was sitting across from me, he offered me a chair, and he asked me what my name was and I replied. He asked me whether I knew him, and he told me to look at him. I looked at him but I could not recognise him. He was shaved. He looked -- he sort of had a short, military-like haircut. He did not have a beard. He did not have a moustache. I did not recognise him. Then he told me that he knew me very well, and I said, "Very well. Very well." I just shrugged my shoulders. I didn't know what to say. Then the interrogation started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just tell me, by topics, what did they ask you about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: First they asked me most of all about my family, my husband's family, where my husband was, where his brothers were, where were the brothers' sons. He asked me about people whom he knew, and he mentioned to me that he knew them as well, and that I should know them too and that they were family friends sort of. I answered the questions I knew answers to, and if I did not know the answers to some questions I said I didn't know, and then they faced me with an ultimatum. They said, "You have five minutes to give us an answer," and then they started counting. They said they were strict about this and that if I did not answer within five minutes' time that there would be consequences, something to that effect, as if they would kill me. I said to them, "I told you what I knew and what I don't know, I don't know. You can kill me. I stand by what I said, and I cannot answer what I don't know." It lasted for quite a long time. It seemed like an eternity to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right, Witness K. We're now going to move to the next passage. We can deal with this quite quickly, because I'm going to ask you a couple of questions, and if I get it right you can simply say "yes" or "no" to me and we can move on. Is it right, just yes or no, that at the end of this interrogation you were asked if you wanted to go back, what you wanted to do, and you said you wanted to go back to the hospital and you were taken back to the hospital? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that in the early hours of the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to ask you to deal in any detail with what happened at the hospital, because I don't think it's of particular interest to the Judges dealing with this particular case. Later that day, were you, with two other nurses and a doctor, taken back to Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you got there, did you go into one of the offices where there were some men and, I think, one woman present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but I'd just like to say that before we got out of the hospital, as we were awaiting, I saw -- it seemed to me that the entire area around the hospital, the park, the compound, was covered with heavy arms and ammunition. I was amazed by this large quantity. I mean, I was shocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Well, then we get to the room. The men in the room, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: In police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The woman, did you know the woman by name at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know the woman but I knew her mother. I knew her mother very well. The entire town knew her mother very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The woman's name was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Monika. Monika. She was a young girl, about 17 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of the men, did one speak and did he introduce himself? On this occasion try to keep it short, but just tell us what he said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man who was sitting by the corner, he wasn't really a man, he was a young-ish man, and he behaved as if the world was his oyster. He introduced himself as Goran Jelisic, the "Serb Adolf," and that we were now in his hands, that the law was in his hands, and that he had a major task, that the Muslims were reproducing to a great extent and that he had a lot of work to do to cleanse us, to create a free territory for the Serb people. May I just have a moment? Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could give her a glass of water. All right. Take a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he hated Muslims so deeply that he wanted to kill all of them, with pleasure, that he had got a green light from the International Community, the Red Cross, that there was no hope for us, that our fate was in his hands, and that it was only up to him when our turn would come, and if any one of us were to survive by any chance, by any chance, he said, we could only be their slaves, clean their toilets, serve them. We could not by any means do anything professional. So he underlined several times that our fate was in his hands and that he wanted to do that with pleasure, to cleanse us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then did he do something with another person, a man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Then he ordered to bring in a civilian from the hangar to show us, by way of an example, how great his power was and what he had available to him. He sent for a policeman to bring in a civilian, and he said to us that we cannot look this civilian in the face but only in the feet or, actually, so that we could just see him being beaten up. He just wanted to show his own power and to instil fear in us, and that he could rule our bodies and our fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to the civilian who was brought in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: They brought him in. We had to bow our heads, and I saw feet or legs up to the knees. I saw that this was a civilian, and by the build of his body -- I mean, I couldn't tell at that point, but much later, it was my estimate that this was a very young man, judging by his physique. Goran then ordered, as he was sitting there, ironically -- or, rather, he was screaming to the remaining four that they should surround the civilian and start beating him. Automatically they started beating, first with batons and with rifle butts, and kicking the man. The victim tried to protect himself. He tried to protect his head, and he was screaming and he was begging at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just stop for a moment. Would you like us to take a break so that you can rest for a few moments? Would you prefer that, Witness K?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I waited for seven years to say this. It was very hard. It was very hard to watch, to watch this helplessness, powerlessness, and that we could not help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When the beating had finished, what happened to the man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say a few words before that? I had a feeling that our souls, our souls were being driven out. The man fell down; he was unconscious. I could not see his face because they were still around him. So he fell down and he had his back to the floor. Then Goran ordered to pull him out by his arms, and they pulled him out, and he told them to finish him off; that is, to kill him, to finish him off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After that attack, did you stay in that room or were you moved to another room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they dragged him out, we heard gunshots because it's very near. It wasn't more than a metre or two away from us. He told us that this was only just the beginning and it was merely an example of what was in store for us. He also said that when he caught my husband, he'd do the same thing to him, and then he ordered to take us out to another office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you stay in that other office for some time, but were you then taken again back to the first office where there were some men waiting for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken back or, rather, four of us were taken back to a small room. Before the war, it was a small office, I suppose, for some clerks, junior clerks, very small. We had to sit in a corner. We had to squat in a corner because there was no room for all of us. The furniture was office furniture there. There was very little room, and we all sat in a corner, huddling together with our legs put up. Of course, we huddled together to try to calm down, to support one another. It was a great shock to us all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you called for again and taken back to the first office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we never even managed to calm down. Dark was falling, and a man entered again with a big torch lamp aiming it at our eyes and keeping it like that for five or ten minutes, completely blinding us so that we did not know where we were going. Then he would kick us with his foot or, rather, with his boot, and he told us to stand up very rudely and follow him. Of course, after this strong light, we hit against everything because we could not see where we were going. So we tried to grope our way around, tried with our hands to see where we were going and trying to follow the man who came to fetch us. So we were taken back to the office, to that same office where we had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was there on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same team: Goran, naturally, sitting in a corner; Monika sitting next to him. She was behaving -- ironically, she would also put in an ironic word here and there, but Goran was so -- he was so blood-thirsty. He was speaking in such a voice that froth was coming out of his mouth. He was yelling at us. All his veins in his neck came out, and he was showing all his power, his force, his strength, to instil fear in us, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What things was he saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then he turned to me mainly, saying that he hated Muslim women, that he never wanted to touch a Muslim woman, that they were very dirty, and that he wanted to exterminate them all, but that he hated men more, so that they wouldn't proliferate. In that sense, he said that he would start from men, to avoid any proliferation, to cleanse easier for room for the Serbs, and that he was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did something then happen involving another man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He again ordered another policeman to go back to the hangar and bring in another man. He also told us to put our heads down, and shortly afterwards, a man came, and the same procedure was repeated, the same way, beatings, the same procedure. The man was screaming, of course, trying to protect himself with his hands, until he fell to the ground unconscious and remained there lying down unconscious, and the four of them were waiting to see if he would move again. They were waiting for his movements. Then he ordered again to drag him out and to finish him off, and then again we would hear another shot. As soon as they dragged him out, we heard a shot, and it resounded very strongly because it was in our vicinity. Then Goran would come back again and say that he was a very busy man because there were very many Muslims and that there was a lot of work to do and so that they needed to take us back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Take just a second to look at that map that the Court can see but won't be shown to the public gallery. Take your time and see if you can point out, with any accuracy, the room where Jelisic and the others saw you and beat the men. See if you can point that one out to us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then can you point out the room where you and the other women were being held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. On this occasion when you were being taken back to that room --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- was there somebody there, and, if so, what was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us to this tiny room; that is, that other room where we were before. We were taken back there. There were four of us from the hospital who were taken there. We stayed there; we were alone for a brief moment. We tried to calm down. The window was open, and beneath the window on a chair a guard was sitting. It was a very small room so that we could overhear the conversation between the guards. We sat again in the same corner. I can show it to you. This corner here [indicating]. This desk, it was quite big and it was near the window, so that we had very little room in this corner. We again sat down to try to calm down, but not much time passed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you there because there's one thing I forgot to ask you about in relation to the previous encounter with Jelisic. Just answer this question yes or no. Did you at the time know where your husband was? Just yes or no. Did you at the time know where your husband was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Jelisic say anything to you about your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he'd do his best to catch him. As a matter of fact, when he asked me where my husband was, I told him that I did not know, that we'd gone to work together and that I stayed there and that he went to his business and after that to his workplace, and after that, we simply lost contact. I didn't know where he was, and I was really afraid what might happen because I had no idea where he was. We completely lost contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Back to the room in which you were with the other women. Were you subsequently taken from that room by someone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a short interval of time, the soldier came again with that same torch lamp and again aimed it at our eyes for about four or five minutes, and again kicking us. He told us again to follow him and come out. As a matter of fact, he pulled me by the hand and told me to stand up. I again thought that we were going to go through this same thing, that we'd again see the same thing, and I'd been through that twice already. So I stood up and followed him to the passage which was very narrow. At that moment when I was in the passage, as I came out into the passage, he pulled me -- he pulled me into another room for all he was worth. I mean, he just pulled me in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you point out on the plan which room you think it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This room [indicating], he pulled me into this here. Well, it was opposite --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Opposite, all right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you got into that room, was something happening there that you could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a very small lamp there, so it was in semi-darkness. I saw a woman, I knew her name was Zena, and I saw her lying down. I saw a soldier sitting, looking as if he'd finished whatever he was doing -- what he was doing, at that moment, she told me not to try to defend myself, to just yield to avoid beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was happening to her? Did you see or did she tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that her face was all blue with bruises. There were so many bruises you couldn't see her face, all around the eyes, the whole face.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was actually happening to her? Just tell us in a sentence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I didn't know what had happened to her. I mean, at that moment, I saw what had happened, but I didn't know about the bruises until she told me later that she was at home, that it was terrible, that they came, they looted, looking for gold, for a car, and after that, they threw a blanket over her and beat her and then the whole group, to the last man, raped her. All those who were in her house, there could have been ten men, I don't know how many, but there were a large group of men, and the bruises originated then. In that room, I saw by the posture that she was in and by the soldier above her, I knew that it was a rape. Those were fleeting moments. At that moment, it could have been a couple of seconds, I saw her, and then I was pushed into another corner, behind the desk, and then the same -- he embarked on the same procedure with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm only going to ask you about two or three questions, and you can answer them with probably single-word answers so that you don't have to go into the detail unless you choose to or want to. In the attack on you, was it one soldier or more than one, and if it was more than one, just tell us the number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three of them, three soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just yes or no to this: Did you do your best to resist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did what I could. I crossed my legs, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't need the detail, you see. You've told us all I need to know, that you did your best to resist, but in the event --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying. I was trying to resist. Physically, I was trying very hard, but they had no sympathy. They had come with that purpose in mind, to indulge in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last question, which again you can answer, if you like, with just one word, is how many of the three men in the event succeeded in raping you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After that had happened, were you returned to the other rooms? If you were, I want you to tell us what you could hear afterwards, after you'd been returned to the room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they finished, the two soldiers, the third one was cueing there, and the door opened, and there was a group of soldiers and they called them to go into action. They told them that they had to get ready quickly and go off to an action. So it was all like a lightening. They left in a matter of seconds, and I stayed there lying down. I simply could not stand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you return to the other room or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that night, did you hear any sounds from the man Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned for a moment to my room and I saw there crying a detainee, like a child, and he was apologising for not being able to help us because he wanted to give us support.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This detainee, although we don't need his name, was he a professional man, and if so, what was his profession? But don't give his name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a gynaecologist and an obstetrician.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You stayed there that night. What did you hear from that man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have time to calm down. We could hear shouting and yelling. He was moving at a lightening speed towards the hangar, ordering about people to bring in. I could hear his voice; I could hear his words. I think you could hear his voice a kilometre away; he was yelling that loudly. I saw him take out a group of people from between the hangars and the office where we were, in this direction where we were when we -- in the office where we were first, where we were interrogated. I can show it to you. It was somewhere here [indicating]. There were three or four lines of people lined up, and I was watching, of course. We couldn't watch for long because there was a guard there, but the voice shouting and the gunfire were horrendous. So naturally we could not but look through the window at least on the sly. We simply wanted to see what was happening to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you see happening or what did you hear from those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ordered them to sing Serb national songs, with a Serbian accent, and to sing it very loud. There was -- I mean, he was moving as if he was running around between those lines listening to each of those individuals to hear if he was singing loud enough, if the accent was as he wanted it to be. We could hear gunfire. It was horrible to look at that. We could hear every word of each and every song. We could hear every word which he yelled, except that I can't recall them right now, but these were nationalistic songs. He moved between those lines, and then he would come back to the hangar, and he would go back to those lines, and it took quite awhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the next topic I want you to deal with, which we can deal with maybe quite shortly, is in completely general terms what you did or were made to do in the next few days or weeks, so we can get a very quick picture of what happened to you, and then I'll deal with just a few things in detail. Now, do you understand what I'm going to ask of you? Just yes no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So over the next few days or weeks, were you kept in Luka? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you obliged or made to do certain jobs in the course of the daytime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did those jobs include cleaning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And also preparing food for the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the cleaning include cleaning the lavatories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you obliged to clean the lavatories by hand or were you given any equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: By hands. There was nothing, and there were no tools, no aids, nothing, with our hands only. There could have been an old broom or, rather, only the stick, the handle of the broom. So you couldn't do anything. You had to use your hands. There was nothing else. It was disgusting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At night -- and I'm now going to turn to what happened to you at night. Did you -- paragraph 26 for the time being. At night did you ever go to Jelisic's office? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it some nights, most nights, or every night? Most nights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Jelisic's office, in the evenings or nights, what happened? Again, you can deal with it, if you find it possible to deal with it, you can just deal with it in a sentence or so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same things happened over and over again. They would bring people in front of us, beat them. Same principle as the first night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did the beatings end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: The victim would be unconscious, without moving. Then they would drag him out and Goran would order to finish the victim off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of these things, did Jelisic say anything about himself? Did he give a name for himself? Did he say anything about the people who he was having beaten up and killed, anything of that sort? Again, if you can deal with it shortly, just do. Just tell us in summary.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: About himself, he said that he was the main figure in the camp, that everybody had to respect him, that he was responsible for all that was happening, that he was issuing orders, that he wielded out fates, that he decided about fates, and he repeated time and time again that he was a "Serb Adolf" -- the "Serb Adolf", that he was copying the Nazi method of cleansing people. People obeyed, that people were obedient, they obeyed him, that they did all that he would order them to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say what was to happen to the Muslim people who survived, what they were to be doing in society?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he would do his best to cleanse the territory for the Serb people so that they would have more room, and that it was his duty to cleanse as much as possible, and if any Muslims survived, he said "if," that all he could do was cleanse -- that that Muslim could only exist to do menial jobs, to be a slave, that is. In other words, that we could only be their slaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, of course, had been -- were trained as a midwife. Was anything said about your particular future in terms of occupation or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me that I should not dream of going back to the hospital again, that I could only clean their lavatories or something like that, that I did not stand a chance of ever receiving permission to go back to work in the hospital again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. So that's part of what happened in the evenings or the nights while you were detained at Luka. Paragraph 30. Did anything else happen to you, not involving Jelisic but involving other soldiers, in the nights that you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other soldiers who screamed terribly at civilians. There was shooting. It was so loud all over. It wasn't only Jelisic, there were other people who wanted to do that, who entered the hangar, got out of the hangar. There was shooting, there was beating. People in the hangar screamed. It was horrible to listen to that. On the other hand, it's not a big town. A lot of detonations could be heard, and shooting behind our backs, behind the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's probably my fault, but I don't think that you necessarily heard my question, or perhaps I didn't ask it very well. While you were detained there, at nights did anything happen to you involving other soldiers? Did other soldiers do anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean whether the same things were repeated as in the room, like the first night?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, but the next time I was there alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, was it one other night, some other nights, most other nights --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- all other nights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When these attacks on you were made, was it by one soldier, or more than one soldier, or did it vary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly there would be more of them, two or three or four. It depended. It wasn't always the same. The soldiers the next time would have an accent like people coming from Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes or no, if you can; did Jelisic himself ever take part in any of these sexual attacks on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he ever physically present at any of the sexual attacks on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but he said that whatever happened in the camp, that he was responsible for that, and that he was the man in charge, and that he had to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We come now to the cleaning of the offices. Two points. First, when you cleaned the rooms, just generally, did you find on the walls and perhaps on the floors, from time to time, certain stains and signs of something? If so, what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that room where there were beatings taking place, there were bloodstains on the wall, on the floor. So we'd have to clean that up in the morning. Actually, we had to clean every room, room by room. We would first start by cleaning up the blood. Then in the other room there would be lots of drinks, bottles, alcoholic drinks, cigarette butts. I think there were hundreds of bottles, bottles from alcoholic drinks, but in this other room we saw blood mostly that we had to clean up. That was the room where people were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next thing in the cleaning, on one occasion did you see a piece of paper with some writing on it that you were able to read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you point out the room on the plan? Right in the middle of the block.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicating]. Yes. Since we went from room to room while we were cleaning, we did one -- room by room in a row, and since we finished this one, we went into the other one, and accidentally I saw some papers on the table. I wanted to dust the table and also to clean the ashtrays while the woman working with me was throwing the bottles out, and as I was dusting and cleaning, I saw on the corner of this table four or five papers. So I accidentally saw, as I was dusting, that this was a list, a list of people, and I saw that these were people to be executed. Then out of fear or curiosity, I can't tell myself, with the speed of lightning I looked through these lists to see who these people were, how many were there. I was trembling all over. I used one eye to watch the door and the other eye to scan the list to see what was on the list by way of information. I would not have even noticed the paper had it not said "People For Execution". Then I opened this, and then I saw in handwriting, in very legible handwriting, I saw names and surnames of people, with numbers by their names. Most of these people were men. Most of them were Muslims. There were a few Croats too. All the pages were filled out. So in my estimate, at that time I could say that there were about 50 people, but I was so afraid and all of this was in a hurry. As I was reading this, it was so fast. It was so fast. I skimmed through it. I would recognise people's names, a lot of people who were well known in town, people who worked in prominent positions, but I didn't have time to dwell on each and every name. I skimmed through the pages one after the other, and I was interested in the number, and I was interested if I could see the names of people I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you leave the pieces of paper where you found them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told you, with one eye I was watching the door so that no one of them would come in and I was looking at the list, because if they saw me doing that, I would have to take the consequences. On the other hand, I left it all as if it had remained intact. I didn't even want to dust it. So I wanted it to seem as if nobody had had a look at it, that nobody had touched it. I didn't want them to suspect me having seen this, not for a moment. I only told my friend, another woman, about this. At that moment, as she was carrying the bottles out, I stood at the door by -- with the bottles so that she would also glance at the lists. This was so fast. It was perhaps half a minute or a minute. She didn't stay any longer than that. She wanted to see these lists so that perhaps she could see this and remember some of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Just a few matters of detail about the period of time that you're talking about and then I'm very nearly finished. First of all, is it right that there was a period of time when you fell ill that one of the detainees was able to get you some medicine and you recovered? Just yes or no to that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many days, roughly, were you ill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three days. I think three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the events you've described, that is, being taken to Jelisic's room to see the beatings, the rapes that you've described, did those events happen both before and after the period of your illness or only before or only after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before and after. While I was ill, I was unconscious most of the time. I had a high fever. My kidneys hurt badly. I didn't have any medicines. I had felt those pains before, but I tried to take it because I had no one to turn to for help. However, the process became worse and the pain became unbearable and the fever went up, so I really got ill. Actually, it was -- I can't remember anything concerning those three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't need anything more than that. I'm just trying to find out the periods of time to which your illness relates. So allowing for a period of three days somewhere in the middle of the overall period when you were ill and indeed semiconscious or unconscious, how long overall approximately were you kept at Luka with the things happening that you've described to the Judges? How many days, how many weeks, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: These terrible things happened around the 19th of May. A group of people had come to the hangar for a visit and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know what you're going to help us with, Witness K, and I'm going to come to that, but if you'd just be so good as to try and answer the first question I asked and we can deal with things in an orderly way. How long do you reckon it was, very roughly, then that these things were happening to you at Luka, 1 day, 5 days, 10 days, 15 days? You tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Luka until the end of the month, until the end of the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So how long altogether were the beatings and the rapes and so on going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. It's my mistake for not asking the question clearly. I want you just to tell the Judges, overall, for how many days these things you described happened, and the things that I'm talking about are the beatings by Jelisic and the night-time rapes and so on. How many days was it? Did it last for five days? Did it last for ten days? Very roughly tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to calculate it, subtract three days when I was sick, then when I was brought in, until the 19th of May then. Just give me a moment, please. Let me calculate this. Let me calculate the time. About two weeks, I think. Two weeks. I was brought in around the 4th. I was ill for three days. On the 19th the torture stopped. About two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next matters are not necessarily in sequence, they're just little details that I want you to provide, if you can, things that I've missed as I've been going along. When you were made to watch people being beaten in the evenings by men in Jelisic's office, were you alone or were other people made to witness those beatings as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other time, if I can remember -- first I was brought in alone. Then they went and brought in the doctor. Then they went out again and brought two more persons, two nurses. So they waited for all four of us to be there. I don't know why they didn't bring us all together, but that's what the procedure was. They first brought me in, and then [redacted], and then two other persons together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That name should be struck from the record. The men who were beaten in the way you've described, were they, so far as you could judge, in military uniform, or civilian uniform, or couldn't you see? Civilian clothes I mean, not civilian uniform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the men who were beaten, the people who were being beaten, the victims?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the victims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- well, those who were doing the beating were wearing police uniform, but the victims were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Then in relation to the rapes on you, what I want you to do, if you can, is to provide any names of men who did these things to you. Maybe you can provide some names in relation to the first rape. If you can, can you give us the names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first name was Stojanovic Mekivija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second name, I only know the nickname, Zuco.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know the name of the third man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you able to name any of the other men who raped you in the course of your time there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wish I could have remembered their names. I wish I knew them, but -- but I can't give you the names when this was so fast. These were different men, accents coming from Serbia proper. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the last passage of your evidence, I think we can deal with very swiftly. Again, in large measure, in large part, I can say something to you and you will probably be able to just say yes or no or to answer with one word. On the 19th of May, you've already mentioned that date, did a military officer come to Luka, and he appeared to be a military officer of high rank? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he in company with that same man, Dragan, who you've referred to at an earlier stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Dragan's other name is -- what's his full name, Dragan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's the first time I recognised Dragan Veselic. His name is Dragan Veselic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can tell the Judges or maybe the other counsel the detail of this, if asked, but all I want from you in one word is, were you and the other detainees able to tell this officer, this high-ranking officer, what had happened? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he promise that the behaviour would stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say that those responsible would be punished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After that, did things change so that the rapes and the beatings stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the most part, was Jelisic absent from the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say, as for myself and for my women friends, it stopped, I mean these terrible things, these rapes and everything when we were under a roof. I cannot guarantee for other people, but I had the feeling that the atmosphere had changed and that less things were heard. After that, I did not see these lineups, the singing, the beatings. So it was a drastic change for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was the person then in charge of the camp, after the 19th of May, so far as you could judge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Kosta, Monika's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you still have to carry on doing cleaning jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you stay in the camp for some more days or weeks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Until you were moved to where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: A building near the SUP, near the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A house, I think --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- where you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a house. It was a house very close to the police station, so it was dangerous to move, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before you finally left Luka, however, had you seen Jelisic again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it once or more than once that you saw him again in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 19th of June, this gentleman said, the one who had a military uniform on, that he would protect us and that he would forbid Jelisic or anyone to enter our room. However, after that, Jelisic could be heard from across the gate, yelling. He was very angry. He wanted to get in, and I think the guards didn't let him, until he jumped over the fence at a given point in time. He ran in at the speed of lightning. Our window was open, we did not expect anything, and he ran in our room through the window, threw himself at the table. He was so enraged; he was so blood-thirsty. He just needed a minute; he just asked for a minute. However, the guards reacted very fast, and they pulled him by the legs, and he said that he just needed one minute to finish us off. He called us vipers, whores. I think he was very angry because he was denied certain things; he did not manage to indulge in the things he wanted to do. So it involved quite a fight to get him out. He was frothing at the mouth. He wanted -- if he only had one minute, the minute he asked for, I think he would have done all of that. That's the state that he was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes the questions I want to ask of this witness in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to take a half-hour break to allow the witness to regain control of herself before she is asked questions by the accused's defence counsel. You were very courageous, and I ask the Victims and Witnesses Unit to take care of her and to do what's necessary. We will take a half hour, and if there's any problem, the registrar will inform me. We will adjourn and resume at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Do you feel all right, Madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did have some rest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Greaves cross-examines, I realised that I completely failed to deal with the lists, and I must deal with those. There's also one other question that I should have asked the question, a matter of detail, and I'd like to deal with that. I understand from Victims and Witnesses Unit that there may be something that the witness herself wishes to address to you, the Chamber, but I must leave that to her. I've explained the position to Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, one other matter of detail, Witness K, that I should have asked you about. You told us about a woman who was being raped when you first went into that little room, the woman who told you about how she was arrested and taken from her home and so on. Can you tell me this, please: What was the occupation of her husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was a lawyer. That is what she told me and that is how Goran treated him, as a lawyer. Ironically, that was the end of his law career, that he was taking over his role, that he was now to be both judge and lawyer. That is how I know that he was a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that man, the husband of the woman, also detained at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give me any part of the name of the woman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zena Vatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness please, in the private session that we have to follow, have the two lists, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For completeness, Witness K, I should have asked you about your own husband. Did you and your own husband meet again after you were transferred in September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had he, in fact, been detained during the time you were detained or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Has he since died in an independent -- in an accident or an event that happened some years later, an explosion, I think?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know if it was an accident, but I know that it was the -- there was an explosion at the police station where he worked, when he was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nice. Witness K, you know, I'm sure that you were told, you are going to be asked questions by one of the Defence counsel for Goran Jelisic. I don't have to repeat this to him, but I call upon his sense of responsibility to protect, at all times, the witness's dignity. But I must tell you, Madam, that this is a judicial institution. An accused has the right to be defended. It is under those conditions that the cross-examination will be conducted, which will be done by Mr. Greaves, I assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague has reminded me -- excuse me, Mr. Greaves. Perhaps you would wish to make a statement. Of course, you can make any statement that you wish, Madam. So it is with no reluctance at all that I authorise you to make the statement that you wish to make, if you want to, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I really wish really to confront Goran Jelisic. I've waited seven years for that. I went through a horrible experience, and I needed all my courage and all my strength to come here. I'm not trying to be a hero. I felt it was my duty. It is my feeling that he has many more privileges in this Tribunal than we had in the camp. If he cannot walk, let them bring him and carry him in. I only want to see his eyes. Perhaps for my recovery in a way, I don't know, but I really do feel the need to confront him, to look him in the eyes. I do not want to say anything to him. I only want to look him in the eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me turn to Mr. Greaves and Mr. Londrovic. Do you have any news about Goran Jelisic? Will he be able to participate in the hearing this afternoon? What do you think? Possibly, could you encourage him to be here for the testimony which, in fact, is very particular? Can you use your influence so that he might be able to come? Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I called the detention unit during the break. I talked to Goran, and I was told that he was examined by a doctor and prescribed some medicines. I am also told that he will give his blood for analysis, and both he and the doctor hope that he will be well enough tomorrow to come to the trial. I fully understand the wish and the courage of Witness K. As far as I understood, Witness K does not wish to have cross-examination in the absence of Goran Jelisic. We can respect that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to add something else, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness K, just a moment, please. Mr. Londrovic -- let's let him finish. I'll give you the floor again, but let Mr. Londrovic finish, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm ready, if I may, to use another break to call Goran Jelisic and to ask him if he feels well enough and if he can to come here. We really don't like his not being here, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor back to Witness K and then I would like to consult with my colleagues. Thank you, Mr. Londrovic. Thank you very much also for this assistance that you are bringing to help the victim find serenity. Witness K, did you wish to add anything before we deliberate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to add as regards one's state of health, perhaps my health is much worse, but my pain and all that I went through forced me to come here. They simply -- I felt compelled. I didn't sleep for nights. Nobody ill-treated him. I think he can come if I could come after all that happened, and I really request that he comes. I want to see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I'm going to consult with my colleagues. I would like to say two or three things to you myself personally and as a Judge. You see, what you experienced is what one could call the most serious expression of barbarity, and here I hope that we will be able to use the most highest and laudatory expression for an institution represented in civilisation. We have noticed many times, and I am reassuring the Defence that -- let this be in the transcript -- I'm only relying on the guilty plea of Goran Jelisic to the crimes that he committed, but we can see that Goran Jelisic -- he has the right to leave the courtroom, whereas you did not have the right to leave the hangar. That's all that I can say. As for the rest, we are doing our labour as Judges. I thank Mr. Londrovic for the suggestion that he's going to make. I'm now going to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges are going to suspend the hearing so that they can deliberate more than they could at the bench. This will also allow the Victims and Witnesses Unit to take care of Witness K. I will again ask Mr. Londrovic to please confer with his client about the points that have been discussed and to know, among other things, whether his client will come this afternoon. We're going to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Without any further ado, I would give the floor to Mr. Londrovic, who I think has some information to give us, and I thank him for having made all the arrangements necessary in order to reach his client. Mr. Londrovic, could you tell us what you have learned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague, Mr. Greaves, and I have established telephone contact with Mr. Goran Jelisic. We explained the situation to him. We advised him to make an extraordinary effort, in spite of his illness, to come because this is absolutely requested by Witness K, and he is going to make an extra effort and he promised that he would come in this afternoon. But now what should be organised is bringing him in from the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Londrovic. We will resume this afternoon at 3.00, not at 2.30, but at 3.00, which will allow time for Mr. Jelisic to come. I would like to now turn to Witness K. What you've asked is, in fact, quite a substantial request. This is a request which puts into question many principles of all types and of very high values, the principles of justice and those principles which deal with the complaints of the victim, but also principles which put into question issues dealing with the rights of the accused. Since here this is one of the fundamental rights, that is, the right to be ill, this is Mr. Jelisic's right, and he has a medical certificate, he's been examined by a physician, and we Judges cannot question that certificate. In this respect, I believe it was confirmed to me that the physician would go to see the accused before he comes here. That's why we set the time at 3.00. If he cannot come this afternoon, even though he would desire to do so, and that matter has been confirmed by his representative as counsel, at that point, I believe that Mr. Jelisic will be here tomorrow morning. We will discuss the conditions under which the cross-examination can take place with Mr. Jelisic, and it is self-evident, Madam, that the Judges will not make any comments to him about what you have said because he is also protected by justice, as you are. That is what I can say for now. Therefore, in principle, the hearing is postponed until 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.12 p.m. 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Mr. Greaves, I was going to take the floor, but I see that you wish to speak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. If Your Honour wanted to say something, then I will sit down, but there is something I have to draw to Your Honours' attention concerning the matters that we discussed just before lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply wanted to speak about Mr. Jelisic. Did you want to speak about as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That was what I was going to speak about. So perhaps Your Honour better start and then I'll follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. First, we'll -- all right. First, we'll listen to the Presiding Judge, that seems a natural thing to do, and then if we really have to supplement things, we can do that as well. With all seriousness, let me turn to Witness K. Mr. Jelisic is not going to come. Mr. Jelisic has been told by the doctor that he must not come. He has been forbidden to come. I ask you to understand, Witness K, that under those conditions, I do not have the power, Judge Rodrigues does not and Judge Riad does not have the power, nobody has the power to require or even ask, even for a worthy cause, cannot force a human being, even if you think many things about that human being, which we respect, he cannot be dragged into this courtroom. Therefore, Mr. Jelisic will not come, and we the Judges, we take the responsibility and we say that he does not have to come, but he will not come most likely tomorrow either. He must undergo medical examinations, and the medical certificate indicated that he could not come tomorrow either. Under those conditions, and in respect of the powers that we have pursuant to the Rules and the Statute, in order to ensure a proper trial, we have decided to proceed with the cross-examination. I remind you nonetheless, with all the respect for what you asked for, that first of all we did what we could do in order to understand your reasons, and I also take advantage of this moment to thank the Defence for having understood also, beyond their professional duties, which are to defend a human being, for having tried to understand your position. I remind you as well that you were able to see the accused yesterday, not very much, I understand, but you did see him. Lastly, you know that this is an accused who, about a great number of facts, pleaded guilty, that he acknowledges what he did. I am convinced that our decision does not fully match what you had wanted, but I hope that you will understand it. Mr. Greaves, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm afraid I've got a spanner to throw into the works concerning what Your Honour has just said. Can I tell you what the information that we have is and our instructions are? The defendant, as you know, prior to lunch was asked if he was prepared to come to court, and when my learned friend, Mr. Londrovic, spoke to him, he indicated that he was prepared to come to court. That decision was communicated to the authorities at the prison, and my instructions are that an official at the United Nations Detention Unit took it upon himself to prevent the defendant from coming, indicating that he, the official, was not prepared to take the risk of a sick prisoner being brought to the court. The defendant indicated that he nevertheless was still willing and wanted to come to court and was prepared to take the responsibility for so doing, and my learned friend, Mr. Londrovic, has spoken to the defendant since that passage of discussion took place and has confirmed that the defendant still wishes to come to court. I understand there may have been a fax sent by the official to the Tribunal, to the Registry, concerning that matter. That places us in this difficulty: The defendant, on our present instructions, wishes to come to court, is willing to come to court, and has prepared himself to take the responsibility, despite his illness, to come to court, and that raises the difficulty for us of Article 21. The defendant having indicated that he wished to be present, and those are our present instructions, he is entitled to be present, and that poses, to me, an insuperable difficulty. Those are our instructions. He wants to come; he's entitled under the article to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I wasn't sure whether Your Honour was going to ask the registrar something or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I will ask him a question. The registrar has to confirm what was said to me, that there is a prohibition from the physician. That's what I wanted to be sure about.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that there was a certificate from the doctor saying he should not come. After the deputy at the detention unit had said that he would not allow him to come, the physician agreed with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I add one or two things? Before the short break, when I was approached by the Victims and Witnesses Unit with their understanding of the witness's position, I was told that the witness had said she was prepared to wait as long as was necessary in order to confront the defendant, and I don't think she actually said that when she was addressing you. It may be something you'll need to explore with her or would want to explore with her. The second thing is we do have another witness here today and, in any event, could interpose other witnesses tomorrow were there to be consent of the defendant to those witnesses proceeding in his absence until such time as he is present, should that be the Court's decision, and the cross-examination of this witness could continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I add that I don't know whether his wish to come to court is selectively only in respect of this witness or is a general wish. So that may pose a difficulty through calling another witness until we can establish precisely what the position is, but it's somewhat unsatisfactory as to our present state of knowledge in that regard. I'm sorry to raise that difficulty, but it seems to me a major difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have decided that for this afternoon we will begin with a new witness for the direct-examination. For tomorrow morning, we will ask the registrar to be sure to inform us whether Mr. Jelisic can be present at 10.00 in the courtroom for the cross-examination in the presence of Witness K. Mr. Jelisic's presence in the courtroom, of course, is subordinated to the establishment -- to the drafting of a medical certificate authorising him to come here into the courtroom and to be present for the cross-examination. Of course, Mr. Jelisic will have to repeat the authorisation which he's given and to state that he wishes to come for the cross-examination. Having said this, Madam, and that will be all I have to say, if tomorrow morning Mr. Jelisic is here with a medical certificate attesting to the fact that he can be present for the cross-examination, at that point your cross-examination will begin tomorrow morning. However, let me tell you, if tomorrow morning Mr. Jelisic is not in a position to take his place in the courtroom, we will continue with the cross-examination without him. Have you understood me, Madam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand it. After all, I work in health, and I understand that the other party does not feel well, but I should like Your Honours to understand my fears. I also have very grave health problems, and if I can find enough courage, summon enough courage with all the pain that I feel and with all my health problems, if I could summon enough courage to come here -- and it is really not wished anything else as this for seven years, just an ordinary meeting, without a conversation, without a threat. I'm quite an innocuous person. I do not wish to hurt anyone. But through this pain that I feel through my injured soul and all my ordeals that I went through. This would perhaps help me recover. Could you perhaps look at it from my point of view?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, for the time being, I suggest that we no longer discuss this. The Judges have listened to all the arguments and have also taken into account your own. The Judges cannot make an accused available to a victim. The accused is under the protection of the Tribunal, as are we, and we also protect the witness. We have discussed this over a great deal of time. Mr. Jelisic is sick. He has a medical certificate. No matter what you may think, he is ill and we cannot -- this is a civilised institution. We cannot drag an accused into this courtroom if he is ill, nor can we wait indefinitely for him to get well. Let me point out to you as well that each time that he is absent from the courtroom, we ask the Defence and Mr. Jelisic if they agree to continue. These are the rights of the accused. I know what you're going to say. You're going to say that he trampled on the rights by trampling on the rights of victims, but that is the work of justice. The work of justice is not perfect.
