We know this very well, but we try to render it as perfectly as we can. I ask that you understand this. Therefore, tomorrow morning, Mr. Registrar, you will come to inform me, and we will begin at 9.00, and you will tell me, if necessary, we will interrupt the examination of the witness and we will begin with the cross-examination of Mr. Jelisic [sic] on the twofold condition, that he be in agreement and that he have a proper medical certificate stating that he is in a position to follow his trial. For the time being, Madam, try to find some peace with that explanation. You have stated everything that you had to say. In addition, you know that Mr. Jelisic has also pleaded guilty to almost all of the acts. This is a trial for genocide. I believe that you must try to find some peace with that. We can say nothing further. All the arguments were heard, and I ask, with all the precautions that are required, that the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. Try to relax this afternoon, try to feel better, and we will see one another tomorrow, in any case, for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, can we introduce the next witness? That would be Witness L.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness, Witness L, is available. Mr. Tochilovsky would or will be taking him. As a matter of clarification, are we to understand that the Tribunal has rejected, I think, Mr. Greaves' effective application that the matter should stand adjourned because the defendant doesn't consent, at the moment, to proceedings continuing in his absence? That's my understanding of Mr. Greaves' application or position, unless I've misunderstood it. I felt I ought to confirm that the Court had had that application in mind and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. Would you have wanted another authorisation from Mr. Jelisic perhaps, Mr. Greaves? Is that what you wanted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Given his express wish to attend the trial, the position was that it was not specified in the information that we were given that it was selective; in other words, that he only wished to attend the cross-examination of the last witness. The information we have is that he wanted to attend the trial. That's why I raised the difficulty that we did not know whether it was only in relation to the witness who had requested his presence or that he was prepared to come for her but not for this witness. That was the difficulty I raise, and that's why I said, and that's why my learned friend has got up to confirm the position. It's not so much an application, it's my merely telling you what our instructions are. The difficulty that I was raising was we don't know if he's consenting to a specific part of the trial going on in his absence -- sorry. I phrased that very badly -- whether he was expressing a wish to come for one part or generally. I don't know what the answer to that question is, and that's why I said we don't know whether you can properly continue in the absence of a specific answer to that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to reread the certificate that Mr. Jelisic provided. The cross-examination might have only lasted for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that to resolve the problem, we put on the ELMO, so the interpreters can interpret this, the statement that has been signed by Mr. Jelisic. It will show us that it is of a general nature. Somebody should read this text out loud. Who can read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you allow me to do it, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The translation that has been provided to us leads as follows: "With great respect for the Trial Chamber, the witnesses and all present in the courtroom, I, Goran Jelisic, state that on this day, 9th of September, 1999, and until further notice, I wish the trial to proceed without my presence due to my serious health problems. I'm taking this decision in the request that nobody should change it. Yours faithfully ..." The original is signed in the manner of the Yugoslavs "Jelisic Goran," and is dated the 9th of September, 1999. Your Honour, can I draw Your Honours to the particulars of what it says? It says "Until further notice," and he has, on the face of it, given further notice of what his intention is. That further notice doesn't say, one way or the other, whether it's only for one witness that he wants to come or in general. So I think what -- my learned friend quite properly raised the difficulty again, that we don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Riad? I have no question here, but Judge Riad would like to raise a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, there was no further notice. Your learned colleague contacted the accused for a very specific issue; namely, that witness, Witness K, wished his presence and he said that he would like to be present. So there was a specific issue, and the first notice is still varied. So this was not a notice. It was an agreement to be present for this very witness. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That certainly is a way in which one could properly look at that. I'm just being excessively cautious. I'm not trying to be difficult, but I don't want to get into difficulties if the defendant then turns around and says, "Well, I wanted to be here, come what may," and then blames me or my learned friend for that, and that's the only thing I'm concerned about. I know that my learned friend's concern is that if we continue without establishing the position precisely, that something will be done this afternoon which might render this trial a nullity, and he's being, I suspect, extremely cautious as well. I hope I've read his mind right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, and it's all to your honour that you are working so cautiously with your client but I remind you that Goran Jelisic referred to witnesses, witnesses in the plural. Therefore, we must interpret the fact that this morning, there was an unexpected event, which no one could have foreseen, that is, the request of Witness K. In order to try to respond to that, we are isolating that incident, but I consider that the general provision, as stated by the accused himself, gives you full authority to continue without him in the courtroom. That seems very clear to me. In regard to the semi-threat of this being a nullity, which often I hear in some of the words that are said, is not something we've heard for the first time, but we are conscious of what we are doing and we always base ourselves on our texts, which are our best bulwark, in order to defend lawfulness in this Tribunal. Therefore, I believe that the Judges will interpret this provision as they have interpreted it, and without any further ado, we will continue with the examination-in-chief of Witness L. Do you hear me, Witness L? First, we're going to ask you to acknowledge that the name on this piece of paper is yours, but don't state your name. Do not state your name. Usher, please show it to him. Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Nods]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to take an oath and then after that be seated. Please read the declaration which is being given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. You understand that the accused is not in the courtroom because he is ill, and a medical certificate was produced to that effect. You are going to first be asked questions by the Prosecutor, Mr. Tochilovsky, and after that by the Defence. Perhaps tomorrow morning, the continuation of your testimony, if it does not finish this afternoon, will be somewhat disturbed for reasons which will be given to you but which would be premature to explain to you right now. Mr. Tochilovsky, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: May I have the usher's assistance in placing the summary of the witness statement in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness L, you had an opportunity to read this summary and recognised it as a correct summary of your statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: You read the summary and you recognised it as a correct summary of your statement; is that correct? Please answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Mr. L, were you and your neighbours arrested on May 4, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were you then taken to a house near the white mosque in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How many of you were detained in that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: About 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What ethnicity were those detainees, those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were you then taken to the JNA barracks the same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How many people were there in the barracks when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: A couple of hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were you then put on buses and transported to the Laser Bus Company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How were you treated by guards in the barracks, in the Laser Bus Company? Very shortly, just characterise how you were treated by the guards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Poorly in the barracks, and in Laser, fairly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to those guards who treated you fairly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: They were removed and others came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: In the Laser company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What happened to you or what did you witness when you were in the Laser company, and what happened there approximately at midnight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It was Wednesday evening, around 1.00. A group walked in consisting of a few men, and one of them used a big baton to hit the table. We were all startled, and he said, "My name is Goran Jelisic, called Adolf the second. The first one was in Germany, Adolf Hitler, and I'm number two." Out of his pocket he took out a piece of paper and read the names. Among us was Dr. Kemal from that list whom they took out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How many names were on the list? How many names did he read from the list, approximately, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Perhaps 10 or 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether those names, if you knew those names, were those names belonging to people of the same ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: On Friday, May 8th, were you taken to the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How many people were there? How many prisoners were in Luka when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Almost half of the hangar, perhaps 300 to 400 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: The man who introduced himself as Adolf in the Laser company, had you seen him in Luka upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Just shortly, did you witness the killing of two brothers from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness L, do you remember the date when you were released from Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, in the morning, Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night before your release?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Opposite the hangar, in an office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Who else was in that office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: On my right-hand side, in an armchair, lying in an armchair next to me, Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: So you spent the night in the room where Goran Jelisic was. Can you tell the Court what happened during that night? What did you witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I can. I saw that throughout the night, they were taking men out of the hangar, bringing them to this office. They had to kneel, cross themselves, and write on a piece of paper whatever they knew about extremists, who worked with weapons, for the defence of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What happened to those people who were interrogated after the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: They were taken out. Sometimes shots would be heard; sometimes they wouldn't. Interrogations would go on until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Again, very roughly, if you remember, how many shots did you hear that night, when people were taken out of the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Perhaps 10 to 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: When you were in that room, and there was a soldier who entered the room, or soldiers, what did they try to do to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: They ordered me to get up. One of them slapped my face, and at the very same moment, Goran Jelisic got out of the armchair and threatened them that no one dare touch me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did they obey him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What was Goran Jelisic's position, from your impression, from what you saw? What was his position with regard to other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I saw that, and it was as if he were stronger than they were or that he ordered them or something like that, since they did not dare oppose him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you see Goran counting money in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did he make any comments in this regard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. He showed me an amount of money and said that a man had given him money so that he would not kill him, and he said, "I took the money and I killed him nevertheless."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you remember any comments, Goran Jelisic's comments about the morning coffees he has every morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me that in the morning, when he would get up, before he would take his coffee, he'd have to kill 20 to 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was that comment made by him the same night, in the same office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was there an attorney from Brcko among the prisoners in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was his wife also in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what you know about this couple in Luka? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: The attorney's name was Osman Vatic. He was a disabled man. He used to be a very good swimmer. A corpulent man. For a few days, together with his wife -- for a few days they allowed him to spend the day with his wife and in the evening they would put him into the hangar with us. Then throughout the night he would walk with one foot only because he only had one foot, and then we would hear him all night. Often they would take him out, they would beat him up badly, and several times he was returned to the hangar unconscious. His wife was in those offices all the time. She was never in the hangar. When he was transferred from Luka to Batkovic, they let him go home, and I heard that they killed him at his own threshold.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you know what was happening to his wife when she was in the office building and he was in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: While we were there, while we were in Luka, in addition to his wife there were two other women. On one occasion, one of the guards in the hangar told us that they were below us who were in the hangar. Then screaming could be heard. What happened over there I cannot say, because I didn't see it for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How did the lawyer, the husband, react to that at night when he heard all this screaming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Several times he cried. He sobbed, but it didn't do him any good at all. He could not have changed the situation at all. Not only him, but not any one of us who was there at the hanger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness L. We can move to the lists. The first one is Exhibit 12.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Mr. L, you said that Goran Jelisic, when you were in the office room, he told you that he killed the man who gave him the money. What else did he tell you about what he did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I don't know. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did he mention anything about the bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he had put 750 kilograms on the bridge and that he was the one who blew it up, and he said that on Radak bridge, there were 450 kilograms of explosives which he also put there, and that he put 750 kilograms on the Brcko bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: You also mentioned that two brothers from Zvornik were killed and you witnessed that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you remember who killed them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When we came from Laser, at the entrance to the hangar, we all had to empty our pockets and take off all that we had around our wrists, whether watches or jewellery or things, and when we were in there, Goran entered and called out for two men from Zvornik to come out. As they were coming out from the crowd, he began to beat them and took them into the office, and when he came out of the office, he continued beating them, and they were imploring him, saying "Why? Why?" And he killed them both. Then he went back into the hangar and said that they were Green Berets and snipers at the Kula, at the tower in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you describe the place where those two were killed? Where were they killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: The place where there was the manhole, at the exit, as I come out of the hangar between the offices on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you describe how the second brother was killed? What was Goran Jelisic's behaviour, how he behaved, when he killed the second brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: In cold blood, showed no mercy whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did he watch the body when he shot? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: He was standing for a couple of minutes next to that, I presume just to be sure that he was really dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to take a 20-minute break, and then the Defence will ask you some questions, Witness L. Please do not move. The Judges are going to withdraw. We will resume at a quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. We will resume our work, and without any further ado, we give the floor to Mr. Greaves. Approximately how much time are you going to need to cross-examine this witness, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Between three-quarters of an hour and an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Three-quarters of an hour to an hour. Perhaps we will ask the interpreters, if we do have the hope of finishing tonight, that we can try to do so, but we'll apply this flexibly and within reasonable limits. If we can't finish in time, we'll start tomorrow at 9.00. Mr. Greaves, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. L, I'd like you to start, please, by looking at a document, which I think counsel for the Prosecution has.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I had arranged for a document to be ready to show to the witness. Thank you. Your Honour, this should not be placed on the ELMO, just given to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. L, do you see the document that has been placed in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is that a statement which you made in May 1995, I suspect, at the conclusion of a series of interviews conducted between the 17th and the 23rd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Does it contain or does it bear your signature in a number of places, first of all, on the first page --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: -- and then finally with your initials on each page after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If you would please be kind enough to look at page 25 of that statement, does your signature appear on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, does it appear underneath six lines of text which are separated out on the page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. L. Can you help us about this, please: The process by which that document was produced, which is your statement, you were interviewed, and then at the end of that, did you have that statement read aloud to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again for the sake of clarity, the final signature on page 25 accompanies a statement that reads as follows: "This statement has been read over to me in the Bosnian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection. I have given this statement voluntarily and am aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international law, committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991, and that I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal." Do you remember that being read out to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were the matters that you recorded in your statement, as well as you've indicated there, true to the best of your knowledge and recollection, were they also accurate; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. L. I don't need you to look at that at the moment now. Can I turn, please, to this: During the war that we know took place in the early 1990s in your country, did you serve in the military forces of any of the participants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Before the war, did you take any part in politics, whether as a party member or as an activist of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: During or since the war, did you take up politics in any way by joining a political party or becoming an active member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you, you were asked about the summary that you gave, in part of which you refer to events that precede the outbreak of fighting, and I just want to ask you two quick questions about that, please, Mr. L. Prior to fighting breaking out, is it correct that there were, to your knowledge, negotiations underway between the various ethnic groups about the division of Brcko into ethnic areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. There was a meeting at the cultural centre, and the SDS, SDA, and HDZ met there to agree that Serbs should get the centre, Srpska Varos, and the industrial area. The meeting was to be resumed on the 4th of May, but it was never resumed because the war had broken out already.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was one of the participants in that process the mayor of Brcko, Mustafa Ramic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, and he kept telling the citizens of Brcko on the radio and television that it was peace, that there would not be any war, and people who were fleeing from the war, they were coming into our town and they were crossing our bridge, which was still in one piece, and nevertheless, the mayor continued, saying that there would be no war. So some people had already left the town of Brcko and came back; some unfortunately stayed there forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. L, I want now to move to an incident which, I think, you became aware of on April the 30th. Did you become or were you awoken by a detonation, which, in due course, proved to be an explosion at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, Thursday, the 30th of April, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you, in due course, go to the scene of what had happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I took my vehicle to go there to see what had happened because I, my family, and the whole town were awakened by the detonation, and we jumped out of our beds. My wife thought that it was a plane crashing down, but I immediately thought that it could be the bridge, and I went there and I saw bodies of people scattered all around.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Does it come to this: that the bridge, the physical structure of the bridge had been very badly damaged, and some three buses, fully loaded with passengers, had been caught in the explosion that had taken place on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, because on -- in the night between Wednesday and Thursday, three buses had come from the place called -- come to a place called Vunja on the Croatian side, and every night, because every night the bridge would be between 10.00 at night until 5.00 in the morning. So at about twenty to five, some women and children had asked our side to let them through. When our side let them through and when the other side saw they had been let through, they let those come onto the bridge, and the explosion took place at the moment when a large number of people were between those two pillars of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct: that in that incident that a large number of people had been either killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I remember that perhaps 100 to 200 people were on that part of the bridge at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of those 100 to 200 people, a large number were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Only a few were transferred to the hospital for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you now, please, about your evacuation or your going to the medical centre. I'm sorry. Let me start that again. It wasn't a well-asked question. I want to ask about May the 3rd and 4th. Were a number of people from the -- I'm sorry, my pronunciation is not very good -- Mujdenovaca of Brcko made to go to the medical centre and the mosque near the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. It's opposite from the mosque, and the medical centre was there and that's where they were taken, the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to just briefly go into a private session because I'm going to deal with a name which is, in fact, on the list, but it comes convenient at this particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: (Open Session)

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Turning now to Monday, May the 4th, Mr. L, you were taken, I think on that occasion, in a column of something like 40 people, towards the white mosque. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, to Dr. Sajdovic, a gynaecologist, into his big house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think that doctor had gone elsewhere before the events of May 1992 and his house was empty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct: that there was something like between 200 and 300 people gathered at the house when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. There were so many that I was practically at the door. Not anyone else could fit in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The 200 to 300 people and the people in your column, were they of all ages and sexes or were they just men? Can you help us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, men, women, and children, and old men, and young people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to go into private session for reasons similar to the last private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Having been at the house for something like two hours, is this correct: Transport arrived and the women, and children, and those who were not of military age were separated from those who were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The women, children, and the men who were not of military age, were they taken -- do you know where they were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No. No. That moment we did not know. They only said that they were taking them to a safe place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Those who remained at the house, about 80 to 100 men, is this correct: that they were selected for detention, their continued detention there because they were considered to be militarily capable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You were then taken to the barracks, and in due course --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: -- were you able -- when you were at the barracks, did you become aware that there was shooting taking place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, there was shooting taking place. A lot of shooting was taking place. So we kept saying that we should lie down, duck, and get up, and then lie down again, and then get up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct: that you were able to -- or you concluded that what was taking place was sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, because they started shouting when they told us to lie down, that snipers were shooting and that they could hit us too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct: that in the -- what then took place when this sniper fire broke out, you were able to conclude that the Serbian military people had been caught very much by surprise by the outbreak of that firing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. They were caught by surprise too, because they probably didn't expect that shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think you were given information about where the women, and children, and the elderly were going to be taken. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. They were supposed to be taken to Bjeljina or Razljevo. My wife and children were brought in, and also my sister-in-law and her children, and I said they should go to Bjeljina rather than Razljevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In any event, to cut it short, your family were taken away and the other women and children were taken away that day, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and old men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How many people did that leave at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I imagine between 200 and 300, because three buses were taken, and they would load as many as people as possible into every bus, as many as could be in there standing or sitting, and they had a military escort as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Subsequently, Mr. L, were you -- at about 8.00 or so, did you end up at the Laser Bus Company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You were placed in a building which had, before the war, served as the works canteen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct: that the canteen building is divided into two principal parts, one the sort of eating hall and a second smaller part at the back of the building which are the kitchens and storerooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. These guards that -- Dragan said that everything that was there available could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The people who were detained there with you, were you kept in the main part, the eating hall part, or in the -- in both parts of the building or only in the kitchen part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: In the eating hall part. The women and children were in the office of this head of the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct, Mr. L: that the -- as the evening wore on, it became dark and some emergency lights were put on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Four of them in all, which gave off a dim yellow glow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Presumably it was difficult to see what was going on in the canteen by such light?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've described to us someone coming and calling himself "Adolf" in that conversation. Had you ever seen that person before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In the canteen, how far away were you from the person you claimed said that? How far away were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Forty-five metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help me, please, about this: Is this right, that the description you gave of the man Goran Jelisic to the Office of the Prosecutor read as follows: "He was 26 to 27 years old; approximately 180 centimetres tall; had medium length light brown to blonde-coloured hair; blue eyes; weighed 68 to 72 kilograms; and had a well-proportioned, medium build"? Do you recall giving that description of Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That's the description that you put in your statement in May 1995, a statement which you have described as containing accurate information? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, 100 per cent, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How did you learn the name "Goran Jelisic," Mr. L?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: As soon as we were transferred to Luka, and that night, when he came, he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: See, what I must put to you, Mr. L, is that the person you describe as Goran Jelisic cannot be Goran Jelisic because of the inaccuracy of your description, and let me explain exactly why. Firstly, Goran Jelisic, in 1992, did not have light brown to blonde-coloured hair, and, secondly, far from having blue eyes, he is a man with brown eyes. I, therefore, put it to you that you have got the wrong person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you should rephrase that question because you're affirming things which one would then assume would have to be developed. So please reformulate the question. Try to be more nuanced or else bring out an evaluation which would show what he looked like. I don't think that we can allow ourselves to say to a witness, "What you're saying is wrong because I, Mr. Greaves, assert that he is as this and that." I don't think that you can -- I'm sure that you can rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If Your Honours would just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. L, would you accept that it is possible that you have got the wrong person when you describe Goran Jelisic as having those characteristics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, I did not make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If the person that the Court, the Tribunal, knows as Goran Jelisic, in fact, turns out to have brown eyes, that would be different, would it not, from the person you have described as having blue eyes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I was where I was, I said what I said, and what I said is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If we have a picture here at the Tribunal of what is acknowledged to be Goran Jelisic and it shows that he had brown hair, again that would be different, would it not, from someone with light brown to blonde-coloured hair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I'm certain of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tochilovsky?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence allege that -- if we have a picture, and then he said that the accused Goran Jelisic would look in the picture such and such a way, in this case, the picture should be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm perfectly content that that should be so. I think it's Exhibit 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The criterion of the hair is not absolutely the criterion. It's not because you're wearing a wig today which says that the colour of your hair is something that it might not be. The colour of the eyes is one element, but you have to go to the very end of what you're trying to demonstrate at the proper moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like the picture to be shown? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm dependent on the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, do you have that colour photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I don't have a photograph, unless I've misunderstood something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think it's described as a copy of a photograph which had formerly been published by The Washington Post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in colour, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It wouldn't be a very useful exercise if it was in black and white, and I wouldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is a photograph which shows two people from the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, the photograph, have you seen it? This is the photograph that's being shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you see that photograph, Mr. L?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you see the man on the left whose back is towards you with, I think, a bandage on his arm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, Goran.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the colour of the hair which we can see in that photograph is not light brown to blonde?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: That's the way it was to me at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In due course, you were taken to Luka. Did you arrive at Luka on May the 8th, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, after noon, after 12.00 on Friday, the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How many nights in all did you spend at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Only one night on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you got to Luka, were you the first people to arrive there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No. There were very many people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In the group that you were with, brought from the Laser company, how many were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Three buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What, about 150 people, 200 people; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Well, between 200, 250, 300 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is it correct that you entered the Luka facility through what might properly be described as the rear entrance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Having arrived with the buses, did the buses go to, as it were, the last hangar before you go out of what is, I think, the other entrance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: The last hangar from the rear entrance into Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I wonder if you could have a look at a photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Just give me a moment, please. It's that photograph. It's the aerial view of the Luka facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm grateful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Now, Witness L, I think there's a pointer, which you will have put in your hands by the usher, and if you could use the pointer to indicate as I ask my questions of you. Don't lean forward because that may involve you being seen on the television cameras. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Could you please, by pointing to the photograph that is there to your right, indicate where it was that the buses on which you were being transported came to a halt and from which you then got off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: They came here [indicating], they stopped here [indicating], and we boarded off here [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So right outside what is the door to the hangar, which is at the end of that group of hangars.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't need you to point any more at the moment. I may want to ask you some more questions. Having got off the bus, did you go --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, this is in respect of the organisation of our work in respect of the interpreters. At what time did we begin the cross-examination, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fear my estimate may have been slightly out. I gave it a bit quickly, and I may have been slightly wrong, so I've still got a little bit to do with this, and it may be a little more than I thought, just so that you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what I would also like to tell you is that very frequently you go back to points that are not challenged by anybody. I mean, the buses that were stopped there were never challenged by your client. Therefore, you must also try to take into account, even if ordinarily you have the right to conduct your cross-examination as you like, which is a right which is absolutely recognised to you, but I also use the Rules and the Statute in order to be in a position to conduct this trial as I understand how it should be, that there are imperatives that must meet one another on both sides. When there are elements which have been more or less established, one must not go back to them in great detail. The buses arrived at the hangar; I think this is something which has been acknowledged more or less, even if it were nothing more than the plea of guilt, and I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Sometimes one wants to establish whether or not a witness is in a position to see something or inspect something and then one wants just to find out whether he saw any particular things. Perhaps I can just develop it a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. L, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has already answered. I can point out to you that these are questions that have already been asked. Continue, but try to focus your questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. L, how long was it that you were standing outside that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: As soon as we alighted from that bus, at the entrance into the building, there was a table, and two men were standing by this table, and we had to empty our pockets and take off our watches or rings or whatever we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to look at the building which was the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was there anything about the building which struck you as being unusual or any damage to it that you noted at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: There were no window-panes left on the building after the detonation at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: For example, on either side of the door to that end hangar, the walls, had they been damaged in any way at the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I've finished with the photograph. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to stop in five minutes for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I ask that your time be limited tomorrow. You must focus your questions, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. L, during the course of the 8th of May, were people being released as well as brought in to Luka that you could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. About 80 to 100 people were released that day. They were issued passes to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you see the passes that were being issued? Can you describe them, if so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It was about that big [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So about eight or nine centimetres by six; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from physically seeing the size of it, did you see what was written on any of the passes? Did anybody show you one that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were you interrogated at all that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I was not because I spent the whole night in the office, and Goran Jelisic was next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you become aware of two particular police inspectors at the Luka facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. There was Dragisa from the police, who used to work with files, and Petar Kaurinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct: that those two men were employed as criminal police inspectors with the SUP in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were they conducting interrogations of people who had been detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were they in charge of those interrogations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Whether they were in charge or not, I do not know, but I do know that they were police inspectors and had come there with the files, allegedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I interrupted you and I apologise for doing that. Did you hear from any of the other prisoners what it was they were interested in in the course of the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Others told me that they acted like judges there. But what questions they asked, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: They acted like judges in that they decided who it was who was to be killed and who was not to be killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm coming to another topic. I wonder whether that is a convenient moment at which to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is an appropriate moment to stop. All right. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00. About how long do you think you're going to need tomorrow morning, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm going to try and cut it down overnight, if I may, and I would hope to finish in under 20 minutes, if I have an opportunity to cut it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreter said "20 years." I think that was a mistake in the interpretation. The interpreters are tired. Twenty minutes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I need to go through the list, and that will make it slightly longer than 20 minutes. I'm sorry. I'm quite tired as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're starting with the idea of 40 minutes, and let's try to keep it more or less at 20 minutes, which would then allow us to know whether Mr. Tochilovsky has any further questions, and then I'm sure that the Judges will have a few questions to ask. Then at 10.00 -- I mean, in the meantime, we will have news from Mr. Jelisic, either he will be here or he won't, and in any case, we will conduct the cross-examination of Witness K. Court stands adjourned. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 10th day of September, 1999, at 9.00 a.m.
